extracted.intended_audience: American colonists and politically-engaged readers deciding on separation from Great Britain (Colonial public, local leaders, delegates)
extracted.subtask_description: A revolutionary-era political pamphlet arguing for American independence and proposing principles and structures for a continental government. It addresses readers' reasoning, rebuts reconciliation arguments, and sketches constitutional and procedural proposals for united governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple facts, plain arguments, and common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The author offers 'nothing more than simple facts, plain arguments, and common sense' and asks the reader to divest prejudice and prepossession and to 'suffer his reason and his feelings to determine for themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should set aside bias, think as a man (not partisan), and enlarge their views beyond the present day; arguments should be accessible, grounded in common sense, and presented plainly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republican virtue versus monarchical corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: The corrupt influence of the crown has 'swallowed up the power, and eaten out the virtue of the house of commons,' so that England's government, though called a republic, is nearly as monarchical as France or Spain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good constitution preserves republican virtue (liberty of choosing commons). Where republican virtue fails, slavery follows; evaluation of governments should consider whether executive patronage has corrupted representative bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that arms have decided the contest; prior plans are obsolete
rubrics_metrics.description: By referring the matter from argument to arms, a new era is struck; 'All plans, proposals, &c. prior to the nineteenth of April... are like the almanacks of the last year; which... are superseded and useless now.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-hostilities, previous reconciliation plans are outdated; policy and evaluation must account for the changed reality created by armed conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconciliation is temporary, dangerous, and insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconciliation would be 'mere patchwork' and can amount to no more than a temporary expedient or guardianship; it risks long-term ruin and unsettled government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh whether the goals justify the cost — a temporary repeal or ministry change is not worth millions and lives; prefer durable solutions (independence) over transient compromises.

rubrics_metrics.name: America's commercial interest supports independence
rubrics_metrics.description: America's commerce are 'the necessaries of life' and will always have a market in Europe; being a free port will secure peace and friendship and protect trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic evaluation: independence preserves markets while avoiding being drawn into European wars; trade self-interest argues against political dependence that risks trade disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on Britain drags the continent into European quarrels
rubrics_metrics.description: Any submission to Great-Britain 'tends directly to involve this continent in European wars and quarrels' and makes America a make-weight in British politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political alignment should be measured by whether it exposes the polity to foreign conflicts; neutrality and avoidance of partial European entanglements are virtues for America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the 'parent country' trope; consider broader origins
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'parent or mother country' applied solely to England is false and narrow; Europe, not England, is the parent country of America, a refuge for persecuted lovers of liberty from many parts of Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments relying on sentimental metaphors of filial duty should be scrutinized; demographic and historical realities (diverse European origins) undermine claims that loyalty to England is natural or obligatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geography and history imply separation is natural
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance at which the Almighty placed England and America, and the timing and manner of discovery and peopling, argue that external authority over the continent was never intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider physical distance and the historical context of settlement as factors in whether continued political subordination is legitimate or practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: A distant monarch's negative over legislation is intolerable
rubrics_metrics.description: If the king retains a negative over legislation, he will prevent laws 'but such as suit his purpose,' keeping the continent low and humble; the king's veto is far more dangerous here than in England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valid government must allow local lawmaking without an external absolute negative; evaluate constitutions by whether they permit self-legislation free of a hostile external veto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distant governance is impractical and inconvenient
rubrics_metrics.description: Governing a continent from thousands of miles away is impracticable: waiting months for answers, petitions, and explanations leads to folly and inefficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess governance schemes for responsiveness and practicality; local conditions demand nearer, more immediate authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: A continent should not be perpetually governed by an island
rubrics_metrics.description: Small islands fit as objects for kingdoms to care for, but 'it is very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island.' Nature never made the satellite larger than the primary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political arrangements that reverse natural scales (island ruling continent) are unjustified; legitimacy and practicality require proportional governance structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence is required to preserve peace and avoid civil wars
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing but independance, i.e. a continental form of government, can keep the peace of the continent and preserve it inviolate from civil wars; reconciliation may invite revolt and civil tumult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate systems by their capacity to maintain internal peace; a continental, republican system with equality is presented as the best guarantee against domestic strife.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of representation prevents supremacy struggles
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect equality affords no temptation to superiority; where there are no distinctions there can be no superiority — republics (Holland, Switzerland) are peaceful compared to monarchies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design representative institutions to minimize inequalities between constituent parts to reduce incentives for internal domination and conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form a Continental Conference to draft a Charter
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose a Continental Conference composed of committees and representatives (26 members of Congress, two members from each Assembly/Provincial Convention, and five representatives of the people) to frame a Continental Charter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a mixed assembly (experience + popular empowerment) to draft fundamental constitutional documents; practical composition and selection methods are provided to blend knowledge and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continental Charter should secure freedom, property, and religion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Charter (analogous to Magna Carta) should fix rules for choosing members, define jurisdictions, secure freedom and property for all men, and 'above all things, the free exercise of religion, according to the dictates of conscience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundational charters must explicitly protect individual rights and set clear institutional boundaries between continental and provincial authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed Continental Congress structure and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Let assemblies be annual with a President only; representation more equal; each colony divided into districts sending delegates so each colony sends at least thirty; Congress at least 390; presidency chosen by rotation by lot among colonies; not less than three-fifths to be called a majority for laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific procedural mechanisms: equalized representation by districts, rotation to prevent dominance, supermajority (3/5) threshold to ensure broad consent; these are concrete institutional design recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leaving government seats vacant—draft a constitution now
rubrics_metrics.description: Form a constitution 'in a cool deliberate manner' while possible; omission now opens the door for a 'Massanello' or demagogue to seize power and sweep away liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize timely constitutional design to prevent power vacuums; delay risks adventurers exploiting disorder to establish tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism: law should be king, not a monarch
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose a ceremony proclaiming the charter with the law placed on the 'divine law' and a crown placed to show that 'in America the law is king' — afterward the crown should be demolished and scattered among the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use public symbolism to cement the principle that law, not personal monarchy, holds supreme authority; rituals help communicate constitutional principles to the populace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure objectives against their expense
rubrics_metrics.description: The object contended for ought always to bear some just proportion to the expense; fighting merely to remove the North ministry or for temporary measures is not worth the millions spent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions should weigh ends against costs; prefer large, enduring objectives (independence) to small, ephemeral gains that demand massive sacrifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and military readiness determine immediate ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Strength lies not only in numbers but unity; the continent now has 'the largest body of armed and disciplined men of any power under Heaven' sufficient for the present aims, though naval strength must be developed later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess readiness by considering unity of effort and existing military capacity; recognize limitations (naval building blocked by Britain) and plan accordingly.
